body.p: In this amendment, claims 1-20 are pending, with claims 1, 10, and 19 being independent. Claims 2, 8-13, and 16-20 are amended to correct minor informalities and antecedent basis issues. No new matter has been added.
Applicant acknowledges, with appreciation, Examiner Park for participating in the

telephonic interview (Interview) conducted on November 16, 2023, with the undersigned. During the Interview, no exhibit was shown; and, no demonstration was conducted. Potential amendments to claim 1 were discussed. The § 102 rejections were also discussed. No agreement was reached during the Interview.
Applicant acknowledges withdrawal of the restriction requirement.

Claims 12 and 13 have been objected to for minor informalities. Claims 12 and 13 have been amended to state the correct statutory category of claim. Those skilled in the art will recognize that claims 12 and 13 have been amended only to correct typographical errors. In view of these amendments, withdrawal of the objections to claims 12 and 13 is respectfully requested.
35 U.S.C. ? 102 Rejections: Claims 1-20
Claims 1-20 have been rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(2) as being allegedly anticipated by U.S. Publication No. 20210150873 to Shouldice et al. (Shouldice).
Claim 1 recites, in part:
passively monitoring the user's breathing with a device during a
predetermined time interval generating sensor-generated signals, wherein the sensor-generated signals include at least one of acoustic signals or motion signals;
identifying one or more breathing modes of the user's breathing by
processing data created from the sensor-generated signals using a machine learning
model; and
responsive to detecting a trigger mode based on the identifying, generating
an instruction adapted to the trigger mode and conveying the instruction to the user
via the device.

The Office Action contends that Shouldice discloses "responsive to detecting a trigger mode based on the identifying, generating an instruction adapted to the trigger mode and conveying the instruction to the user via the device." In support, the Office Action cites to paragraphs 172 and 107 of Shouldice.
Paragraph 172 of Shouldice states:
Any detection of respiration peaks and troughs needs to be aware of

potentially confounding effects, such as the subject making a large movement (such as rolling in bed or moving while driving), if the subject stops breathing (e.g., an apnea) or exhibits very shallow breathing (e.g., a hypopnea). Using sensing that can track location provides a useful means of separating these effects. For example, a roll can be seen as both a high frequency movement, as well as change in location in space. Therefore, subsequent breaths may be higher or lower in amplitude-but still be "healthy" breaths. In other words, the detected amplitude change may be due to a change in the extracted received respiration signal (after down-conversion etc.) strength, rather than a change in the person's breathing. Therefore, it can be seen that this can allow a novel calibration approach, where the detected distance can be used to relate signal strength to depth of breathing (and hence approximate tidal volume). Where no such movement or displacement is seen, a diminution, cessation, or change (e.g., due to paradoxical movement on chest and abdomen during an obstructive event) of a specified duration range can be identified as
abnormal breathing (e.g., an apnea/hypopnea event).
Paragraph 107 of Shouldice states:
Exemplar system architecture of a voice enabled sleep improvement system

using low frequency ultrasonic Biomotion sensing is illustrated in FIG. 6. The system may be implemented with the sensing techniques described herein (e.g., multi-tone FMCW acoustic sensing). A user can talk to a voice activated speaker that was previously activated to monitor the user's sleep. For example, a verbal instruction can query the smart speaker, which is received by a microphone and the query of the microphone signal is evaluated by a processor to determine the content or instruction of the query, to produce an audible report of determined sleep score, respiratory (SDB) events or sleep statistics. Based on the report, the processing of the system can also produce audible advice as to improving sleep, such as by suggesting a therapy device to assist with sleep. For example, sleep related data illustrated in FIG. 8, e.g., a sleep score, time in sleep stages, etc., may be summarized verbally and audibly explained to the user via the speaker(s) of the processing device 100 in response to a query received by the microphone such as "how did I sleep last night?" In response, the processing device 100 may generate

output such as sound/audio via its speaker with data detected by the processing device such as from SONAR sensing. For example, in response, the processing device may generate an audio report explaining: "You slept for a total of six hours and woke up only twice during your sleep time. You had four hours of deep sleep and two hours of light sleep. You had an apnea and hypopnea count of two events."

The paragraphs of Shouldice excerpted above illustrate that while Shouldice detects different types of breathing, as stated in paragraph 107, the report of the user's sleep is delivered in response to a query from the user explicitly requesting the report. By comparison, claim 1 generates "an instruction adapted to the trigger mode [as detected] and conveys the instruction to the user via the device," but does so "responsive to detecting the trigger mode based on the identifying."
Paragraph 138 of Applicant's disclosure states that:
As defined herein, the phrases "in response to" and "responsive to" mean

responding or reacting readily to an action or event. Thus, if a second action is performed "in response to" or "responsive to" a first action, there is a causal relationship between an occurrence of the first action and an occurrence of the second action. The phrases "in response to" and "responsive to" indicate the causal
relationship.

Thus, generation of the instruction and conveyance of the instruction to the user in claim 1 is causally related to the detection of the trigger mode. Shouldice does not disclose or suggest that providing the report is causally related to detecting a trigger mode. Paragraph 26 of Applicant's disclosure states that "a 'trigger mode' is a breathing mode that is associated with an adverse health effect." Instead, in Shouldice, the report is provided in response to a user request.
In Net MonevIN, Inc. v. Verisign, Inc., 545 F.3d 1359, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2008), the Court stated:
We thus hold that unless a reference discloses within the four corners of the

document not only all of the limitations claimed but also all of the limitations arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim, it cannot be said to prove prior invention of the thing claimed and, thus, cannot anticipate under 35
Because Shouldice fails to meet the test set forth in Net MoneyIN, Shouldice does not disclose or suggest the features of claim 1.
Applicant's remarks supporting patentability of claim 1 are relevant to claims 10 and 19 and are hereby reiterated in support thereof.
Claim 2 recites, in part:
wherein the identifying is based, at least in part, on determining phases of
the user's breathing, and wherein the determining comprising:
receiving acoustic signals generated by an acoustic sensor in response to the
user's breathing;
generating acoustic data comprising features extracted from the acoustic
signals; and
determining phases of the user's breathing by classifying the acoustic data
using an additional machine learning model, wherein the additional machine learning model is trained based on signal processing of motion signals generated
by a motion sensor in response to human breathing motions.

Claim 2 clarifies that the identification of the one or more breathing modes is based, at least in part, on determined phases of the user's breathing (i.e., inhalation and exhalation at paragraph 27). Claim 2 clarifies that the phases of the user's breathing are performed using an "additional machine learning model." The additional machine learning model determines phases by classifying the acoustic (e.g., sound) data extracted from acoustic signals. The additional machine learning model is "trained based on signal processing of motion signals generated by a motion sensor in response to human breathing motions." That is, the phases of the user's breathing are detected using a machine learning model that was trained based on signal processing of motion sensor data as opposed to being trained exclusively on acoustic data.
The Office Action contends that Shouldice discloses the "determining" operation and, in support, cites to paragraphs 140 and 192 of Shouldice. At paragraph 140, Shouldice states:
Thus, in some cases, the processing device 100 may use motion detection
(e.g., Sonar) techniques for detecting respiration. However, in some cases, acoustic analysis, of an audible breath signal at the microphone, may be implemented by the
processing device 100 for the detection of respiration.
At paragraph 192, Shouldice states:
Further analysis of extracted features can make use of a deep belief network

(DBN). Such a network is composed of building blocks of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM), Autoencoders, and/or perceptrons. A DBN is particularly useful to learn from these extracted features. DBNs can be used without supervision, and then later trained with labeled data (that is, data confirmed by a human expert
input).

Neither paragraph 140 nor paragraph 192 discloses or suggests the features recited in claim 2 as to the particular workings and training of the additional machine learning model. Paragraph 140, for example, only acknowledges that motion detection and a microphone may be used but does not discuss using both together or any particular relationship between the two. Paragraph 192 only discloses a deep belief network that is trained. Paragraph 192 does not describe how the deep belief network is trained, let alone a process that resembles that recited in claim 2. Accordingly, claim 2 patentably defines over Shouldice.
Applicant's remarks supporting patentability of claim 2 are relevant to claims 11 and 20 and are hereby reiterated in support thereof.
The remaining claims are believed to patentably define over Shouldice in view of their own merits and their dependence on the underlying claims.
In view of the foregoing, withdrawal of the 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(2) rejection of claims 1-20 is respectfully requested.

Independent claims 1, 11, and 19 have not been amended. In this Amendment, Applicant submits tenable remarks in support of patentability that differentiate between the pending claims and the cited references. Accordingly, any new ground of rejection that may be included in a forthcoming office action for an original claim is not necessitated by this Amendment and such office action may not be final.'

Reconsideration and a Notice of Allowance are respectfully requested in view of the amended claims and the Remarks presented above. If there are any questions, a telephone call to the undersigned is invited.
